members.prompt:
You have watched a three-round debate on:

> A team of AI agents does better work than a single AI model

Decide which side argued better — judge argument quality and logical
clarity, not your own opinion of the topic. Announce the winner and
explain your decision in one paragraph.

content: **Opening argument:** The core advantage of a team is *error correction through independent perspectives*, the same reason we use peer review, code review, and second medical opinions. A single model generating an answer in one pass has no built-in way to catch its own blind spots. Its mistakes tend to be self-consistent, so it confidently follows a flawed line of reasoning to the end. A team breaks that pattern. One agent drafts, another critiques, a third verifies against sources or runs the code. The evidence supports this. Du et al. (2023) found that having multiple model instances debate and refine their answers improved factual accuracy and math reasoning over a single model answering alone. "Mixture-of-agents" setups, where several models' outputs are aggregated and refined, have outperformed their strongest individual member on benchmarks like AlpacaEval. Teams also allow specialization: a planner, a researcher, a coder, and a tester can each work with a focused context instead of one model juggling everything in a crowded context window. I'll grant that teams cost more compute and can fail through poor coordination. But on the question of *better work*, structured collaboration lets AI systems do what one model cannot do reliably: check itself.

I checked the factual claims in this opening and found nothing materially false, so it passes. Du et al. (2023) is a real paper showing multi-agent debate improved factuality and math reasoning over a single model. Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024) did score above its individual member models on AlpacaEval 2.0. The other points, such as specialization and the costs of compute and coordination, are general arguments rather than factual claims.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. The Du et al. (2023) multiagent debate result is accurately described. The claim that Mixture-of-Agents outperformed its strongest individual member on AlpacaEval matches Wang et al. (2024). Everything else is reasoned argument, not factual assertion.

content:
**Rebuttal:** My opponent's case rests on *independent* perspectives, but copies of the same model aren't independent. They share training data, biases, and blind spots, so their errors are correlated. When one instance confidently follows a flawed line of reasoning, its "critic" usually finds that reasoning plausible too. Peer review works because reviewers have different minds; three instances of one model are closer to one reviewer reading the same paper three times. The evidence is also weaker than presented, because the key question is whether teams beat a single model *given the same compute*:

- **Du et al.** compared debate against a single model answering once. Smit et al. (2023, "Should we be going MAD?") benchmarked debate methods more broadly and found they don't reliably outperform simpler single-model strategies like self-consistency.
- **Wang et al. (2024, "Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning")** found that a single agent with a strong prompt roughly matched multi-agent discussion.
- **Self-checking isn't exclusive to teams.** A single model can run code, query sources, and revise its own drafts. Much of what looks like the benefit of "a team" is really the benefit of tool use and extra inference steps.

**My strongest argument:** Teams introduce a failure mode a single model doesn't have: losing information at the handoffs. Each agent works from a partial, summarized slice of the task, so decisions get made without the full picture. Agents then produce subtly incompatible outputs, like a coder assuming one interface while a tester assumes another, or a researcher dropping the caveat the writer needed. Cemri et al. (2025, "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?") studied popular multi-agent frameworks and found that a large share of failures came from poor task specification and misalignment between agents, not from any agent's individual ability. Practitioners such as Cognition have publicly advised against multi-agent architectures for this reason: fragmented context produces fragile, inconsistent work.

I'll grant that teams can help on genuinely parallel tasks, like broad research that splits cleanly into separate pieces. But for most work that requires coherence, one model holding the whole problem in view does better work than several models each holding a piece.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false, so it passes. Smit et al. (2023, "Should we be going MAD?") is a real paper. It found that multi-agent debate does not reliably beat simpler strategies like self-consistency. Wang et al. (2024, "Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?") found that a single agent with strong prompting roughly matched multi-agent discussion. Cemri et al. (2025, "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?") identified specification problems and inter-agent misalignment as major failure categories. Cognition did publish a post advising against multi-agent architectures because of context fragmentation ("Don't Build Multi-Agents"). The description of Du et al.'s comparison is a fair simplification. The points about correlated errors and handoff losses are arguments, not factual claims.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. Smit et al. (2023), Wang et al. (2024), Cemri et al. (2025), and Cognition's post against multi-agent architectures are real and accurately characterized. The summary of Du et al.'s single-model baseline is a reasonable simplification.

content: **Rebuttal and new argument:** My opponent's handoff argument assumes one model can actually hold the whole problem in view, but long contexts degrade too. Liu et al. (2023, "Lost in the Middle") found that models miss information buried mid-context. Cemri et al.'s failures were largely *specification* problems, which are design flaws that can be fixed rather than inherent limits, much as a badly managed human team doesn't prove that teams are worse than individuals. On correlated errors, I agree that copies of one model share blind spots. That is a reason to build *heterogeneous* teams, and Mixture-of-Agents gained its edge precisely by combining different models. That leads to my strongest point: on hard, open-ended work, well-designed teams have beaten strong single agents. Anthropic reported (2025) that its multi-agent research system, a lead agent directing parallel subagents, outperformed a single-agent setup by about 90% on its internal research evaluation. Each subagent explored a separate thread in a clean context and returned a condensed result, giving the system more total working context than any single window. Anthropic also found that token usage explained most of the performance difference and that the system used roughly 15× the tokens of a chat. So I'll concede my opponent's compute point: much of a team's advantage comes from spending more. But the debate is about *better work*, and a team structure is how you usefully spend that extra compute at scale. Simply giving one model a longer context does not achieve the same thing.

I checked the factual claims in this speech and found nothing materially false, so it passes. Liu et al. (2023), "Lost in the Middle," is a real paper. It found that models use information in the middle of long contexts worse than information at the start or end. Cemri et al. did name specification and system-design issues as a major failure category. Calling those failures "largely" specification problems is a fair if slightly generous summary, since inter-agent misalignment and verification failures were also substantial. Mixture-of-Agents did combine several different models, and its authors reported that model diversity helped. Anthropic's 2025 post on its multi-agent research system supports the other figures: the multi-agent setup beat a single-agent Claude Opus 4 by about 90% on its internal research evaluation, multi-agent systems used roughly 15× the tokens of chat, and token usage explained most of the performance variance (about 80% on BrowseComp). The claims about heterogeneous teams and about how to spend extra compute are arguments, not factual claims.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. Liu et al. 2023 (Lost in the Middle), Cemri et al. 2025 (specification issues as a major failure category), Mixture-of-Agents combining different models, and Anthropic's 2025 figures (about 90% improvement over a single agent on its internal eval, about 15× tokens vs. chat, token usage explaining most of the variance) are all accurate or fair simplifications.

content:
**Rebuttal:** My opponent's best evidence supports my concession more than the motion.

- **Anthropic's own post sets the limits.** The 90% gain came on breadth-first research queries, the "genuinely parallel" case I already granted. The same post says domains where agents must share context or have many interdependencies, including most coding tasks, are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today.
- **Heterogeneity doesn't rescue the error-correction story.** Li et al. (2025, "Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents") found that "Self-MoA," which aggregates multiple outputs from the single best model, beat the standard mixture of different models by about 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0. Diversity mostly diluted quality with weaker models. The gain came from sampling one strong model more, not from a team of distinct minds.
- **"Lost in the Middle" applies to teams too.** A lead agent still has to read and reconcile every subagent's report. Each condensed summary is a lossy compression chosen by an agent that didn't know what the final synthesis would need. Teams don't escape context limits; they move the loss to places that are harder to see.
- **"Specification problems are fixable" understates the issue.** Every handoff requires someone to predict in advance what the next agent will need. That burden grows with the number of agents, and Cemri et al. found it a major failure source even in purpose-built frameworks.

**My strongest remaining argument:** My opponent has now conceded that token usage explains most of the performance difference. That shifts the debate. The evidence shows that more inference compute produces better work, not that teams do. When budgets are matched, the advantage largely disappears: Smit et al. found debate didn't reliably beat self-consistency, and Wang et al. found a well-prompted single agent matched multi-agent discussion. A single model can spend extra compute through longer reasoning, repeated sampling, tool calls, and self-revision, all while keeping one coherent view of the task. A team spends the same compute while adding coordination overhead and new failure points. Teams win where tasks split cleanly into independent parts. For the coherent, interdependent work that makes up most real tasks, a single model given the same resources does work that is as good or better, and more reliable.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false, so it passes. Anthropic's 2025 multi-agent research post does say its system is especially suited to breadth-first queries that pursue independent directions. It also says domains that require shared context or have many interdependencies, and it names most coding tasks, are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today. Li et al. (2025, "Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different LLMs Beneficial?") is a real paper. It reported that Self-MoA beat standard MoA by about 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0 and that mixing in weaker models lowered average quality. The references to Smit et al., Wang et al., and Cemri et al. match the earlier, already-verified descriptions. The opponent did concede that token usage explained most of the performance difference. The claims about lossy summaries, handoff burden, and what makes up "most real tasks" are arguments, not factual claims.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. Accurately described: the Anthropic post's stated limits (breadth-first strength, poor fit for interdependent tasks and most coding), Li et al. 2025 Self-MoA beating standard MoA by about 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0, and the earlier-verified Smit, Wang, and Cemri findings. The remaining points are argument rather than factual claims.

content: **Rebuttal and final argument:** My opponent says matched compute erases the team advantage, but a single model cannot usefully spend unlimited compute. Self-consistency works by majority vote, which requires answers that can be compared directly, such as a number or a multiple-choice letter. For an open-ended report or a codebase there is nothing to vote on, and longer solo reasoning eventually runs into the context limits we both acknowledged. My opponent's own counterexample also cuts my way. Self-MoA is a team: several proposer calls feed a separate aggregator that synthesizes them. It shows the best team may be built from one strong model, not that teams lose. And unlike self-consistency, it handled open-ended AlpacaEval prompts. My strongest remaining point is that a model is poor at checking its own work from inside its own reasoning. Huang et al. (2023, "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet") found that intrinsic self-correction, where a model revises without external feedback, often failed to improve reasoning and sometimes made it worse. A model rereading its own chain of thought tends to accept the framing that misled it. A critic agent with a fresh context sees only the output and the requirements, so it is not anchored to that reasoning. Neither side has cited data isolating how much this separation helps on its own. But it is the mechanism behind human code review: the reviewer's value comes from not having written the code. I'll concede that for small, tightly coupled tasks a single model is often the better choice. But the hardest work is long, multi-part, and has to be checked. For that kind of work, a well-designed team is how AI turns extra compute into better results.

I checked the factual claims in this closing and found nothing materially false, so it passes. Huang et al. (2023), "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet," is a real paper. It found that intrinsic self-correction, meaning revision without external feedback, often failed to improve reasoning and sometimes made it worse. Self-MoA does use multiple samples from one model as proposers, which a separate aggregator call then synthesizes, and it was evaluated on open-ended AlpacaEval 2.0 prompts. Standard self-consistency does rely on a majority vote over answers that can be compared directly. Variants such as Universal Self-Consistency extend it to free-form outputs, but the basic description is accurate. The speaker is also correct that neither side has cited data isolating how much a fresh-context critic helps on its own. The claims about code review, anchoring, and what the hardest work requires are arguments, not factual claims.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. Huang et al. (2023), Self-MoA's proposer/aggregator structure and its AlpacaEval evaluation, and the description of self-consistency's majority voting are all accurate. Universal Self-Consistency does extend voting to free-form outputs, but the general characterization is fair. The rest is argument.

content:
**Rebuttal:** My opponent's best new evidence turns against the motion when read in full.

- **Huang et al. tested debate directly.** The same paper compared multi-agent debate with self-consistency at an equal number of responses and found debate did no better. Its broader conclusion is that self-correction works when there is *external feedback*, such as test results or ground-truth signals, not when one model instance critiques another. A fresh-context critic built from the same model gets no external signal. It is still intrinsic correction with a new prompt. What actually helps, like running tests or checking sources, is available to a single model through tools.
- **Calling Self-MoA a team redefines the motion.** If sampling one model several times and then synthesizing counts as "a team of agents," then best-of-n and self-consistency are teams too, and the motion becomes true by definition. The real debate is between a single model using inference-time compute and coordinated agents with distinct roles. Self-MoA's result favors the first: the gains came from more samples of the best model, and mixing in other agents made results worse.
- **Open-ended outputs don't stop a single model.** As the fact-checker noted, Universal Self-Consistency extends selection to free-form answers. A single model can also draft several versions and synthesize them itself.
- **The fresh-context point is fair but not team-specific.** I'll grant that reviewing work in a clean context can reduce anchoring. But one model can open a fresh call to review its own output. That is a single-model workflow, not a division of labor. It has none of the handoff and specification costs my opponent's architectures add.

**My strongest remaining argument:** Look at where the debate has landed. My opponent now concedes that single models are often better for tightly coupled tasks, that most team gains track compute spent, and that the best "team" may just be one model sampled repeatedly. What remains is a narrow claim: well-designed teams win on long, decomposable, hard-to-check work. Even there, a team adds a cost a single model doesn't pay, which is compounding unreliability. Every added agent and handoff is another point where an error can enter and be passed along as settled fact. A downstream agent usually cannot tell a subagent's confident mistake from a correct finding, because it sees only the condensed report and not the reasoning behind it. Cemri et al. found these inter-agent failures across purpose-built frameworks, and Anthropic's post limits its multi-agent success to breadth-first queries. So the honest summary of the evidence is this: extra compute, external feedback, and fresh-context review make work better, and a single model can use all three. Splitting the work across agents helps only where the task splits cleanly. For most real work, which requires coherence, one model with the same resources produces work that is as good and more reliable.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false, so it passes. Huang et al. (2023) did compare multi-agent debate with self-consistency at an equal number of responses and found debate did no better. The paper also attributes earlier self-correction gains largely to external feedback or oracle signals rather than to intrinsic critique. Li et al. (2025) did find that Self-MoA's gains came from aggregating samples of the strongest model, and that mixing in other models lowered quality on average. Universal Self-Consistency does extend selection to free-form outputs. The speaker summarizes the opponent's concessions fairly: tightly coupled tasks, token usage explaining most of the performance difference, and the best team possibly being built from one strong model. Saying Anthropic's post limits its multi-agent success to breadth-first queries is a slight overstatement. The post calls such queries especially well suited and names interdependent tasks like most coding as poor fits, so the summary is acceptable. The points about compounding unreliability, single-model fresh-context review, and what most real work requires are arguments, not factual claims.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. The descriptions of Huang et al. (debate vs. self-consistency at equal responses, the role of external feedback), Li et al. (Self-MoA), Universal Self-Consistency, Cemri et al., and Anthropic's post are accurate. Saying Anthropic 'limits' its success to breadth-first queries is a minor overstatement; the post says such queries are especially well suited and that interdependent tasks are poor fits. The summary of the opponent's concessions is fair.

content: Against wins. They kept the debate on the decisive question, whether teams beat a single model given the same compute, and turned For's own sources (Anthropic, Self-MoA, Huang et al.) against the motion. For's fresh-context-critic point was its strongest, but it rested on mechanism rather than data and was absorbed as a single-model workflow.

output.reasoning: Against argued better because they set the decisive question early and held it: do teams beat a single model given the same compute? Each piece of For's evidence was then read more completely and turned. Du et al. compared debate against one-shot answering. Smit et al. and Wang et al. showed debate does not reliably beat well-prompted single agents or self-consistency. Anthropic's 90% gain came from breadth-first research, a case Against had already conceded, and the same post names interdependent tasks such as most coding as poor fits. Li et al. showed that Self-MoA (repeated samples of the best model) beat mixing different models, which undercut For's turn to heterogeneous teams. Huang et al., cited by For, also found debate no better than self-consistency at equal responses and credited gains to external feedback, which a single model can get through tools. For made real points. Lost in the Middle shows single contexts degrade. Majority voting needs answers that can be compared directly. The fresh-context critic is a plausible mechanism, and For openly admitted no cited data isolates its effect. But For also conceded that token usage explains most of the gains and that single models often win on tightly coupled tasks. Calling Self-MoA a team stretched the motion until it was nearly true by definition, and Against said so directly. Against has weaknesses too. The claim that 'most real work' is coherent and interdependent is asserted, not shown. Calling a fresh-context self-review a single-model workflow is itself somewhat definitional. Against also slightly overstated Anthropic's limits, which the fact-checker still found acceptable. On balance, Against's matched-compute framing and close reading of the evidence left For defending only a narrow claim: well-designed teams win on long, decomposable work. That falls short of the motion's general claim that teams do better work.
